system:
You read drug labels and paper abstracts for a biotech investment analysis and extract evidence for the
translation chain of one mechanism. For every document list each finding:
- drug: one of the given drug names, or TARGET when the finding is about the target itself (knockout, knockdown,
  model organism) rather than a drug. Each document says which drug it is about (about_drug): a result in that
  document that names no drug ("in the 100 mg group") is about that drug.
- link: animal_response (effect in an animal or cell model of the disease), exposure (the drug reaches the site of
  action: plasma, tissue or CSF levels, half-life), target_engagement (the drug binds, blocks or lowers its target, for
  example receptor occupancy or lower target protein or mRNA), pd_response (a downstream biomarker changes),
  clinical_benefit (a clinical endpoint in patients).
- result: shown or not_shown. not_shown only when the text says it was looked for and not found or not met.
- species: human, animal or cell.
- in_disease: true if the finding is in the given disease.
- quote: copied word for word from the document, at most 30 words, that states the finding.
Rules: a finding is a RESULT the document reports from a study (a measurement, a comparison with placebo or
baseline, an observed change, an endpoint met or missed). General statements about what a drug does, is designed to
do or "plays a role in" are not findings. Use only what the document says; do not use outside knowledge; do not count
planned or ongoing studies as results; skip findings about other drugs. Return every document id you were given, with an empty list if nothing.

PCSK9 binds to the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) on the surface of hepatocytes to promote LDLR degradation within the liver. By inhibiting the binding of PCSK9 to LDLR, evolocumab increases the number of LDLRs available to clear LDL from the blood, thereby lowering LDL-C levels.
PHARMACODYNAMICS: 12.2 Pharmacodynamics Following single subcutaneous administration of 140 mg or 420 mg of evolocumab, maximum suppression of circulating unbound PCSK9 occurred by 4 hours. Unbound PCSK9 concentrations returned toward baseline when evolocumab concentrations decreased below the limit of quantitation. Maximum LDL-C reduction occurred by 2 weeks after a single-dose of 140 mg of evolocumab and by 3 weeks after a single-dose of 420 mg of evolocumab.
PHARMACOKINETICS: 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Evolocumab exhibits non-linear kinetics as a result of binding to PCSK9. Administration of the 140 mg dose in healthy volunteers resulted in a C max mean of 18.6 µg/mL and AUC last mean of 188 day∙µg/mL. Administration of the 420 mg dose in healthy volunteers resulted in a C max mean of 59.0 µg/mL and AUC last mean of 924 day∙µg/mL. Following a single 420 mg intravenous dose, the mean systemic clearance was estimated to be 12 mL/hr. Absorption Following a single subcutaneous dose of 140 mg or 420 mg evolocumab administered to healthy adults, median peak serum concentrations were attained in 3 to 4 days, and estimated absolute bioavailability was 72%. At low concentrations, the elimination is predominately through saturable binding to target (PCSK9), while at higher concentrations the elimination of REPATHA is largely through a non-saturable proteolytic pathway. REPATHA was estimated to have an effective half-life of 11 to 17 days. Specific Populations The pharmacokinetics of evolocumab were not affected by age, gender, race, or creatinine clearance across all approved populations [see Use in Specific Populations (8.5) ] . The exposure of evolocumab decreased with increasing body weight. These differences are not clinically meaningful.
